summary: The article argues that autonomous vehicles (AVs) face a multi-layered cybersecurity threat landscape and that heavy investment in security is essential as adoption nears at the end of 2023. It covers data volume, AI opacity, fragmented regulation, hacker demonstrations, and the need for human oversight. It concludes that automakers, tech firms, and governments must collaborate, fund R&D, and educate the public.
one_line: An overview of the cybersecurity risks facing autonomous vehicles and why investment, regulation, human oversight, and public transparency are needed.
key_facts: Dr. Emily Foster, lead cybersecurity analyst at AVTech Institute, said "Each layer of connected technology presents unique gateways for cybercriminals."
Dr. Jonas Schneider of the German Automotive Security Organization said on October 15th, 2023 that the average autonomous car will process about 4,000 gigabytes of data per day.
Anne-Marie O'Connor, professor in AI ethics at Stanford University, said on September 23rd, 2023 that AI systems can be opaque and detecting compromise is a challenge.
On November 2nd, 2023, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) released joint guidelines for AV cybersecurity practices.
The ISO/SAE guidelines still need to become enforceable laws that define accountability after a cybersecurity breach in an AV.
Researcher Alexandra Ivanov demonstrated remotely taking control of an AV's braking system using a zero-day exploit in its telematics unit.
Ivanov presented at the Cyber Mobility Symposium on December 1st, 2023, calling the demonstration "a call to action for the industry."
As of September 1st, 2023, several cities worldwide had begun trials of driverless taxis, delivery trucks, and private vehicles.
Possible AV attacks include hijacking sensory data to cause accidents and ransomware that locks users out or compromises a whole fleet.
Michael Richardson of the Center for Automotive Safety advocates a balanced approach combining machine efficiency with human critical thinking and ethical reasoning.
Oversight mechanisms could include remote control centers intervening in real time or mandatory manual override features for occupants.
AI security-focused learning models that are tamper-proof and self-correcting are still at the research stage.
DEF CON's Car Hacking Village brings security professionals and hackers together to expose vulnerabilities in car software.
